title: Exodus, looking back
hook: a bush, a sea, manna, a mountain
tomorrow: is there a prayer for feeling two things at once?

segments.voice: This week, six lines from the top: he goes before you; build on rock; all shall be well; that they may be one; nothing can separate us; and yesterday, meant for good, from a brother who forgave. Today, that brother comes back one more time.
screen: `SIX LINES FROM THE TOP.` → `MEANT FOR GOOD.` → `THE BROTHER, ONE MORE TIME.`

segments.voice: Moving day has its own logic. Most boxes say kitchen or books, and one says do not lose. On the night Israel leaves Egypt, in a hurry, with bread that had no time to rise, Exodus stops for one detail. Moses is carrying something that isn't food or gold. It belongs to a man who died long before.
screen: `ONE BOX SAYS DO NOT LOSE.` → `THE NIGHT THEY LEFT.` → `WHAT IS MOSES CARRYING?`

segments.voice: “And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him.” Joseph had made his family swear it: when God brings you out, carry my bones up from here. So the road out of slavery begins with a promise kept to the man from yesterday's story. Exodus, looking back, is that road. A shepherd sees a bush on fire and not burning up, and says, “I will now turn aside, and see this great sight.” Only when he turns does a voice call his name. The sea opens. In the wilderness something lies on the ground each morning, and the people say, “It is manna: for they wist not what it was.” Wist means knew. They ate a question, and there was enough for each day. Then the mountain, and words that begin by remembering: “I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.” A rescue before a rule. This story belongs first to the Jewish people, and Christians read it too; in the Gospels, Jesus's last supper falls at Passover. Here's the detail to tell a friend: the road to freedom carries a coffin. Leaving and keeping travel together.
screen: `MOSES TOOK THE BONES OF JOSEPH.` · `TURN ASIDE AND SEE.` · `MANNA: THEY WIST NOT WHAT IT WAS.` · `A RESCUE BEFORE A RULE.` · then, large: `OUT OF EGYPT.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write two short lines. First, one thing you're leaving, or hope to leave: a habit, a fear, a place. Second, one thing you'll carry with you when you go, the way Moses carried Joseph's bones. If you pray, offer both lines to God.
Exodus. The road out of Egypt: a bush, a sea, manna, a mountain, and Joseph's bones carried the whole way.
Your line: out of Egypt, with what matters carried along. Two weeks from the top, done.

fork.setup: your cousin is moving abroad for work and feels guilty, as if leaving means betraying the family. which Exodus detail fits best?
options: Moses carried Joseph's bones: you can leave and still carry who you come from.
a real exodus means cutting every tie with the old place.
staying put is always the more faithful choice.
fork.reveal: the road out of Egypt began with a promise kept: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him.

original.note: Greek: a way out, the name of the book in the Greek Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: Exodus is the plagues and the sea.
what it means: a road out of bondage that begins with a promise kept to Joseph.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 13:19 keeps the oath of Genesis 50:25, so Joseph's bones tie the two books together.

chat.says: told pop i think i'm going. he gave me his old choir hymnal "for the road." i cried. now what?
options: Pack the hymnal. Moses left carrying Joseph's bones; you can leave and carry Pop too.
Leave it behind. A real exodus means taking nothing old along with you.
Maybe stay. If leaving hurts this much, it can't be the right road.
chat.meaning: Exodus is a road out, and Moses carried Joseph's bones the whole way. Leaving and keeping can travel together.

manna.meaning: the food that lay on the ground each morning in the wilderness
